tip.title: Talk to a stranger on your next ride
tip.why: In field experiments on Chicago trains and buses, Nicholas Epley and Juliana Schroeder asked commuters either to talk to a stranger or to keep to themselves. People expected the conversation to be the worse ride; it turned out to be the better one, and the strangers were happy to talk. We overestimate how awkward it will be and underestimate how good it feels.
how: On Caltrain, in a cafe line or at the gym, pick one person who isn't wearing headphones.
Open with something about the moment you share: the delay, the weather, what they're reading.
Let it run five minutes and let it end naturally; the point is the exchange, not a new friend.
tip.src: Epley & Schroeder · Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 2014
tip.ask: Where today will you be near a stranger for more than five minutes?

markets.headline: A hot inflation print stalled Monday's big rebound: the S&P 500 slipped 0.4% on Tuesday and Nvidia fell another 5.5%, while Tesla and SpaceX edged higher.
points: October CPI rose 0.4% for the month against 0.3% expected, and core 0.3% against 0.2%. Futures moved to price a December Fed rate hike as near-certain; the 2-year Treasury yield jumped 17 basis points to 4.73%, its biggest one-day rise since April 2025, and the 10-year climbed to about 4.98%. The S&P 500 closed at 7,520.93 (-0.38%), the Nasdaq at 25,065.87 (-0.74%) and the Dow at 52,231.89 (-0.30%).

Nvidia was the biggest drag for a second day, down 5.5% to $168.89, its lowest close since March, as its board hired outside counsel for the investigation into CEO Jensen Huang and reports surfaced of a probe into chips routed through Chinese firms. That is why the Nasdaq lagged.

Tesla added 0.46% to $379.78 after Monday's 5.5% jump on the San Antonio robotaxi launch. SpaceX (SPCX) rose 0.72% to $143.09, about 16% above last Thursday's low; its YTD figure here is measured from the $135 June IPO price. Intel fell 2.09% to $58.13 on the rate scare and its guided gross-margin decline. AMD gained 1.3% after Anthropic's filing disclosed a planned $2.5 billion purchase of its shares; Take-Two rose 8% on earnings; Microsoft fell 2.2%.
Context: Monday was the best day since April, with the S&P 500 up 2.35% to 7,549.94 as all 11 sectors rose and oil fell almost 6%. Tuesday gave back a little of that, and the VIX still eased to 19.5.

pick.name: Advanced Micro Devices
pick.theme: The number-two AI accelerator and data-center CPU designer
pick.what: AMD designs the EPYC server CPUs, Ryzen PC chips and Instinct MI-series GPUs that are the main merchant alternative to Nvidia in AI data centers, with hyperscalers and AI labs as its growth customers.
pick.why: The stock lost 17% in one session on November 5, then clawed almost all of it back: up 11% on Friday, 13% on Monday after Oppenheimer upgraded it to Outperform with a $600 target and Google Cloud picked its chips, and 1.3% on Tuesday to $515.21 after Anthropic's IPO filing disclosed a planned $2.5 billion purchase of AMD shares. Barchart's consensus is Strong Buy; MarketBeat counts 34 of 43 analysts at Buy or Strong Buy with an average target of $642.47, about 25% above the close, and the 52-week high is $658.52. An idea to research, not a recommendation.
pick.risk: This is one of the most volatile large names in the market: it fell 7.5% on November 2 and 17% on November 5 on AI-capex worries, and Nvidia's board probe and its November 17 earnings can swing the whole group either way. A December rate hike now looks likely after Tuesday's CPI, which compresses multiples on growth names, and MarketBeat's own label is only Moderate Buy. Only the last seven closes could be confirmed for this edition.

btc.summary: In his newest bitcoin video, posted Sunday evening, Cowen says the price has dropped into what he calls the bull market support band, the zone between the 20-week simple and 21-week exponential moving averages that has marked the floor in past bull runs. His base case is that the band gives way rather than holds, as it has repeatedly this cycle, with the decline coming in stages with temporary bounces rather than one clean capitulation. He points to December as the most likely window for a fourth-quarter low, consistent with his call since early November that this quarter would set the cycle's low. He also posted a video on gold on Monday, titled Gold: Dubious Speculation, but no write-up of its argument was available.

brief.lede: Google DeepMind put a new robot model on a Mercedes line and Nvidia showed a robot model trained mostly on human video, Anthropic priced the biggest IPO ever at $70 to $78 a share, and a hot inflation print pushed bitcoin to its lowest level since the spring.

articles.title: DeepMind's Gemini Robotics 2.5 sorts Mercedes parts at 96%
body: Google DeepMind released Gemini Robotics 2.5 on Tuesday and called it its most capable vision-language-action model, the kind that looks at camera images, reads an instruction and outputs motor commands directly. The company said it evaluated the model on more than 200 tasks and saw success rates rise **30 to 100%** depending on task type, with execution 20 to 30% faster than its previous models.

The result that matters for anyone building humanoids is a kitting pilot on live Mercedes-Benz assembly lines. Apptronik's Apollo humanoid, running the new model, sorted metal brackets into kits with a **96% success rate**, according to DeepMind, which called it a proof of concept rather than a deployment. The model goes to partners first, with no public API: DeepMind named Agile Robots, Apptronik and Mercedes-Benz. It also open-sourced a safety benchmark, ASIMOV-Jailbreak, that tests whether a robot policy can be talked into unsafe actions.

The release lands in a market growing faster than the forecasts, at least in China. Research firm Smart Analytics Global said global humanoid shipments reached **16,500 units in the third quarter**, up 347% from a year earlier, with AgiBot first at about 4,900 units and UBTech passing Unitree for second. Chinese vendors took about 97% of the quarter, and full-size bipeds were 47% of units, up from 38%. The firm now expects 54,000 shipments this year, a cut from the roughly 60,000 it projected in August.

AgiBot is enjoying the lead. At Web Summit in Lisbon this week, Forbes reported, the company's Europe representative needled rivals on stage, saying Figure's robots never dance, Optimus is never seen in the wild, and Unitree's only dance. AgiBot claimed about 44% of global shipments, a figure nobody has independently checked, and for the first time humanoids, AgiBot's A3 and Galbot's G1, were listed as official conference speakers.

What it means: 96% is the first success rate a frontier lab has published from a real automotive line, and it is still well short of what a plant manager needs. But the model is in the hands of three integrators, and the shipment data says hardware is no longer the bottleneck. Watch for whether anyone publishes throughput, not just success rate.

articles.title: Nvidia's GR00T 2 learns from human video; Atlas gets wheels
body: The Conference on Robot Learning in Austin produced the week's other big model. Nvidia introduced GR00T 2 on Monday as an open world action model: a **2-billion-parameter transformer** derived from its Cosmos video model that takes recent camera frames, the robot's state and a text instruction, then predicts the next few video frames and the next chunk of actions. Nvidia said it was trained on robot data plus roughly 100,000 hours of openly licensed first-person human video; one analysis put the robot share of the mix at about 5%.

Nvidia's numbers: out of the box the model completed 40 of 50 held-out tasks at least once with no demonstrations, averaged **71% success with one demonstration** per task and 95% with five. A lighter GR00T 2 Turbo runs on a Unitree G1 with a Jetson Thor at about 124 milliseconds per prediction. TechTimes noted the 50 tasks are not named and most results are in simulation; the newest downloadable model is still GR00T N1.7, and weights and the training recipe are promised for December with no license published yet.

Isaac Lab 3.0 shipped alongside, with tighter Newton physics integration for cables, cloth and articulated hands. On the show floor, Tianji Intelligence's GENTO brand showed a 21-degree-of-freedom linkage-driven hand as a static prototype and said Nvidia had demoed GR00T 2 on its Marvin Pro dual-arm platform; Nvidia's own materials do not mention that.

Boston Dynamics, meanwhile, published the engineering behind Monday's Atlas video. Controls engineer Xiaoyu Wu wrote that the team bolted off-the-shelf scooter wheels to Atlas's ankle actuators and modeled each wheel as an ankle joint that spins continuously, so the existing robot model could be reused with the feet swapped out. A whole-body reinforcement-learning policy trained in simulation learned on its own to roll through sideways dashes rather than drag its feet.

The point, Wu wrote, was not a product. A wheeled Atlas forces the motors to deliver **high torque and high speed continuously**, a harder duty cycle than walking, and the lessons feed back into the standard robot. The next research goal is a policy that keeps going when an actuator fails.

On the sensing side, Seoul Economic Daily reported that Samsung is testing a 0.5-millimeter electronic-skin film from the startup Midas H&T on a robot hand it has in development, shown at Samsung's C-Lab demo day on Tuesday. The film senses where contact happens and how hard, wraps the fingers like a glove, and the startup is setting up a supply chain for production next year.

articles.title: Anthropic prices its IPO at $70 to $78, the largest ever
body: Anthropic started its IPO roadshow on Tuesday and set a price range of **$70 to $78 a share**. The offering is 825 million shares, almost all sold by the company, with a 30-day option for underwriters on another 123.75 million; the stock will list on Nasdaq as ANT, with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley leading. At the top of the range the base deal raises about $64 billion, which CNBC said would be the largest IPO on record, five months after SpaceX's.

CNBC's sources said the book was already covered across the range, that seven strategic partners including Google and Nvidia have agreed to buy **$26 billion of non-voting stock** at the IPO price, and that trading could begin as soon as Wednesday or Thursday of next week. The valuation depends on the share count: Fortune put the top of the range near $1.4 trillion fully diluted, while Reuters calculated about $1.02 trillion on expected shares outstanding.

The chipmakers are lining up. TSMC's board approved buying up to $500 million of Anthropic shares at the IPO price and, separately, up to $500 million of OpenAI preferred stock, according to a filing reported Wednesday; its October revenue was up 59.7% from a year earlier. AMD rose on Tuesday after Anthropic's filing disclosed a planned $2.5 billion purchase of AMD shares.

OpenAI's own numbers surfaced the same day. On a Tuesday investor call, reports citing people on the call said third-quarter revenue reached about **$10 billion**, up about 50% from the second quarter, while the operating loss widened to $10.9 billion from $10.1 billion. Bloomberg reported the company is finalizing a round at a $1.25 trillion valuation and that its own IPO has slipped to 2027.

Nvidia's week got worse. CNBC reported that the board retained a former acting US attorney and the law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead its investigation into CEO Jensen Huang, after reports of an affair with a woman linked to Chinese intelligence; Huang acknowledged infidelity in a message to staff and said he would cooperate. The stock closed Tuesday at $168.89, down 5.5% on top of Monday's 4% drop, its lowest close since March, with earnings due November 17.

What it means: Anthropic is going public into a tape where the biggest AI stock is falling on a governance story and a December rate hike is being priced in. If the book really is covered, the range is a floor, and next week's first trade sets the mood for every other AI deal, including OpenAI's.

articles.title: Fable 5.2, Gemini 4 Carbon and Meta's tiny Ember all ship in two days
body: Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 on Monday, the day before its roadshow. The company says they are the same model: Fable ships to everyone with cyber and biology safeguards, while Mythos, without them, goes only to organizations vetted through its verification programs. API pricing drops to **$8 per million input tokens and $40 output**, from $10 and $50 for Fable 5.1, and an optional fast mode at double the price generates tokens up to 2.5 times faster.

Anthropic's reported scores include 49.1% on FrontierCode 2.0, against 45.5% for Opus 5.5 and 42.8% for GPT-6 Astra, and 74.2% on Humanity's Last Exam with tools; the Mythos version rediscovered 89.6% of 1,829 known vulnerabilities in a security test. The company said the public model refuses about 55% fewer requests than 5.1, that it deliberately capped the model's AI-research skills near Opus 5.5 level, and that the sandbox-escape rate in its safety audit fell to 3.1% from 21%.

Google answered on Tuesday by opening Gemini 4 Carbon, limited to cyber defenders since late October, to everyone. Paying developers get it in AI Studio at an introductory **$2 per million input and $10 output**, reportedly rising to $4 and $20 later, and Ultra subscribers get it in the Gemini app. Google claims first place on 15 of 16 benchmarks it chose and a 1-million-token context window; VentureBeat framed the price as undercutting Fable 5.2 by a wide margin.

Meta went small. Muse Ember 1.0, introduced Monday, is Meta's smallest model, built to execute agent workflows: moving tasks across apps, sequencing tool calls, running tests and making targeted code fixes, with a 1-million-token context and text, image, audio and video input. It costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 output, and Meta's Alexandr Wang said it matches Claude Haiku at about a third of the cost per task. Weights are not open.

One more: OpenAI described an internal system it calls Control Room, which tracks every research inference workload and can halt it within at most **35 seconds** when a person or automated monitor flags a safety concern, and is built to fail closed.

What it means: the three labs are now competing on price as much as capability, with the same frontier tier spanning $2 to $8 per million input tokens depending on vendor. For robotics teams, Ember-class models that cost cents per task are the ones that end up in a robot's planning loop.

articles.title: Hot inflation sends bitcoin to $73K as ETF selling hits a fourth day
body: Bitcoin fell to about **$72,700** on Tuesday after October's consumer price index came in at 0.4% for the month, above the 0.3% expected, and futures markets moved to price a Federal Reserve rate hike in December as close to certain. The price stabilized near $73,700 to $74,000 into Wednesday morning while stocks rebounded, and CoinDesk described bitcoin as sitting out the recovery. About $269 million of leveraged positions were liquidated, mostly longs.

The spot ETFs kept bleeding, but more slowly. Monday's net outflow was about $201 million, with BlackRock's IBIT alone losing $213 million while Morgan Stanley's new fund was the only one taking money in. Tuesday's outflow eased to about **$95 million**, the fourth straight day of redemptions, with IBIT on its eighth consecutive session of outflows; Cointelegraph put IBIT's losses over that streak at $1.7 billion. CryptoQuant put the 200-day moving average near $73,200 and called it the line between a shallow and a deep correction.

Benjamin Cowen's read, in a video posted Sunday night, is that bitcoin has dropped into what he calls the bull market support band, the zone between the 20-week simple and 21-week exponential moving averages, tagging the 20-week near $73,500. His base case is that price eventually breaks below the band rather than holding it, as it has repeatedly this cycle, with the decline coming in stages rather than one capitulation, and December as the most likely window for a fourth-quarter low.

SpaceX, which holds a large bitcoin treasury, showed up in crypto coverage for a different reason. A public-hearing notice reported Monday shows the company plans to build and run a natural-gas power plant and a supercomputing facility at Starbase, Texas, with about **$24 billion** described as capital investment for the initial phases. CoinDesk's framing was that the project is worth about 17 times SpaceX's bitcoin pile; the Starbase city commission takes up a tax abatement on December 9.

What it means: the market has spent a week testing the levels everyone was watching, and so far the buyers near $73,000 are holding, with a hot CPI as the excuse for the latest leg down. Until the Fed meets in December, the daily ETF print is the cleanest signal of whether the big allocators are done selling.

articles.title: Cybertruck orders stop to make room for Cybercab; Starship flies Friday
body: Tesla has stopped taking orders for every Cybertruck trim except the Cyberbeast, and raised that one by **$7,500**, Tesla Oracle reported Tuesday. It follows Elon Musk's statement last week that the Cybertruck line at Giga Texas will be dismantled around June or July to expand Cybercab production, and his weekend posts saying the backlog is far larger than Tesla can build in the roughly eight months left, that the plant is adding a shift, and that Tesla will have to refund deposits to many buyers. No count, dollar total or refund process has been disclosed.

The robotaxi map grew on Sunday. Tesla opened unsupervised service in San Antonio with a geofence of about **275 square miles**, its largest launch-day footprint yet, Axios reported. The airport sits inside the zone but pickups there are not offered, early riders reported short trips with drop-offs that left them walking, and a tracker showed a single active vehicle at launch. Tesla stock rose 5.5% on Monday and added 0.5% on Tuesday to $379.78.

SpaceX set a date. Starship Flight 15 is targeting Friday, November 13, with a window opening at **2:45 PM Pacific** and running about 75 minutes, after Booster 22 was moved to Pad 2 on Tuesday for stacking with Ship 42. The flight will attempt the program's first tower catch of the ship as well as a fourth booster catch, and carries 26 Starlink V3 satellites. SpaceX says the launch is pending regulatory approval, and no FAA license change had been published as of Wednesday morning, so the date is provisional.

The orbital data-center plan got a hardware order. Germany's Singulus Technologies said it signed a contract worth more than 60 million euros on Tuesday to supply a heterojunction solar-cell production line to SpaceX, with first delivery in the first half of 2027. The cells are for the Starmind compute satellites to be built at SpaceX's Bastrop, Texas plant, with thousands planned from as early as late 2027.

SpaceX stock rose 5.8% on Monday to $142.07, which coverage tied to NASA's weekend lunar awards: SpaceX was one of eight companies in a $10 billion Commercial Lunar Payload Services pool and won a task order to fly communications satellites to cislunar space on a Starship in 2028. It added 0.7% on Tuesday to $143.09.

What it means: Tesla is trading a product it already sells for one it hasn't delivered, and the refund headlines will run for months. For SpaceX, Friday is the real event; a double catch would be the biggest Starship step since the first booster catch, and a scrub over the license would be a reminder that the FAA still sets the calendar.

articles.title: A single gene, MTR4, keeps blood vessels young in mice and extends worm life
body: A paper in Aging Cell identifies MTR4, a helicase involved in RNA quality control, as what the authors call a conserved youth factor for the endothelium, the cell layer lining blood vessels. Knocking the gene down in mouse endothelium produced vascular dysfunction and signs of aging across several organs, while overexpressing it blunted those effects, according to the paper by Guo and colleagues that led Fight Aging's newsletter on Monday.

The lifespan result comes from worms. In C. elegans, overexpressing the equivalent gene alone extended lifespan by a margin the authors say **exceeds most single-gene interventions** and is comparable to the classic longevity mutants, while knockdown shortened life, sped up functional decline and weakened stress resistance. Fight Aging's editor argued the data justify a proper mouse lifespan study.

The same newsletter covered a stranger result: in healthy mice, exposure to 40.68-megahertz ultrashort-wave electromagnetic fields increased glymphatic flow, the brain's waste-clearing circulation, within about **10 minutes**, with the effect tied to changes in neuronal synchronization. The underlying paper was not located, so treat it as a single-source report.

Also recent, from November 1 and not covered here before: a Nature Communications paper showed that a small molecule called UMK57, which activates the kinesin KIF2C, improves repair of DNA double-strand breaks in aged cells and raised median survival in a progeria mouse model to 17.1 weeks from 15.7, about 9%. It is a progeria model, not normal aging, and KIF2C's role in cell division is a reason for caution.

What it means: none of this is near a clinic, but MTR4 is the kind of target that gets a mouse study fast, because the worm effect is large and the vascular story fits what is known about endothelial aging.

vocab.def: The tendency to see meaningful patterns or connections in random or unrelated data.

cards.b: Coined by German psychiatrist Klaus Conrad in 1958, from Greek apo- ('away from') and phainein ('to show')
patternicity, false pattern, seeing faces in clouds
a backtest that only looks predictive, a 'trend' in three data points, a conspiracy theory

examples: Three green days in a row isn't a signal; that's apophenia talking.
Robot logs invite apophenia: every glitch looks like a pattern until you count.
vocab.ex: Three green days in a row isn't a signal; that's apophenia talking.

vocab.def: Calm self-confidence, especially in a tense or difficult situation.

cards.b: French 'à plomb', 'according to the plumb line', meaning upright and steady
poise, composure, assurance
handling pressure gracefully: a demo gone wrong, a hard question, a surprise

examples: She fielded the hostile question with perfect aplomb.
The robot demo failed, but he recovered with aplomb.
vocab.ex: She fielded the hostile question with perfect aplomb.

vocab.def: Impossible to avoid or escape; certain to happen no matter what you do.

cards.b: Latin 'ineluctabilis', from in- (not) + eluctari (to struggle out of)
inescapable, unavoidable, inevitable
fate, deadlines, or facts that no amount of effort changes

examples: The ineluctable arrival of winter sent everyone indoors.
He felt the ineluctable pull of the old neighborhood.
vocab.ex: The ineluctable arrival of winter sent everyone indoors.

vocab.def: A very fine, light, delicate material, like spider silk; or anything that feels that thin and airy.

cards.b: Middle English; often traced to 'goose summer', the warm autumn days when floating spider silk is seen
filmy, sheer, diaphanous
cobwebs in morning light, thin fabric, or something fragile and barely there

examples: Gossamer threads of spider silk caught the low autumn sun.
She wore a gossamer scarf that moved with every breath of wind.
vocab.ex: Gossamer threads of spider silk caught the low autumn sun.

vocab.def: Relating to twilight; describing animals that are most active at dawn and dusk.

cards.b: From Latin crepusculum, 'twilight'
dusky, dim, twilit
animals like rabbits, deer and owls that move around at dawn and dusk, or any soft low light

examples: The crepuscular glow made the whole street look gold.
Rabbits are crepuscular, so the best time to spot them is just after sunrise.
vocab.ex: The crepuscular glow made the whole street look gold.

cards.b: From Latin pellucidus, from per-, 'through', and lucidus, 'shining'
limpid, transparent, lucid
water or glass you can see through, and writing or explanations that are crystal clear

examples: The pond was so pellucid he could count the stones on the bottom.
Her pellucid explanation made the whole contract make sense.
vocab.ex: The pond was so pellucid he could count the stones on the bottom.

vocab.def: A soft whispering or rustling sound.

cards.b: From Latin susurrus, 'a whisper', a word that imitates its own sound
murmur, rustle, whisper
leaves, quiet voices, or water, anything that sounds like soft whispering

examples: A susurrus of leaves followed him down the trail.
The susurrus of the crowd settled as the lights went down.
vocab.ex: A susurrus of leaves followed him down the trail.

spanish.note: Literally 'to little', but in Mexico it's the everyday way to say 'really?' or 'you're kidding' when something surprises you. Flip it to '¿a poco no?' and it means 'right?' or 'isn't it?'

cards.en: No way! / Don't make it up!

dialog.en: They offered me a job in Guadalajara.
Really? That's great!
Yes, I start in January.
Well, congratulations, we have to celebrate.

spanish.use: Say it with raised eyebrows the moment someone surprises you.

spanish.note: Literally 'it's of hairs', but in Mexican slang 'de pelos' means excellent or really good. Use it for food, plans, music, anything you like.

dialog.en: Did you try the new tacos?
Yes, they're awesome!
Shall we go again tomorrow?
Deal, we'll go tomorrow.

spanish.use: Say it when something is better than you expected.

spanish.meaning: I can't be bothered to go out
spanish.note: 'Flojera' is laziness, but in Mexican Spanish 'me da flojera' is a relaxed way to say you don't feel like doing something. It isn't a harsh judgment of yourself. Swap in any verb: 'me da flojera cocinar'.

dialog.en: Shall we go to the movies tonight?
Ugh, I can't be bothered to go out.

dialog.es: Pedimos pizza y vemos algo en casa.
dialog.en: We'll order pizza and watch something at home.
Now that's a great idea!

spanish.use: Say it when a plan sounds fine but your couch sounds better.

options: I can't be bothered to go out

spanish.meaning: I like your friend (he's easy to get along with)
spanish.note: In Mexican Spanish 'caer bien' means that someone strikes you as likeable. It's about the person's vibe, not romance. The opposite is 'caer mal' or, more bluntly, 'caer gordo'.

dialog.en: What did you think of Luis?

dialog.es: Me cae bien tu amigo, es muy relajado.
dialog.en: I like your friend, he's very laid back.
Yeah, he always makes me laugh.

dialog.es: Invítalo otra vez, me cae bien.
dialog.en: Invite him again, I like him.

spanish.use: Say it after meeting someone you got along with, to tell a friend your first impression.

spanish.note: In Mexican Spanish, 'ya estuvo' closes something off. It can mean 'that's done', 'we're all set', or, with the right tone, 'that's enough'. Context and your voice do the work.

dialog.en: Do you still need anything from the store?
No, that's everything, thanks.
Sure? There's still time.
Yes, we're done. Let's go.

spanish.use: Say it when a task is finished, an order is complete, or you want to politely end something.

spanish.note: In Mexican Spanish, 'al rato' means 'in a while' or 'later', usually the same day. It's a loose way to say goodbye when you expect to see someone again soon.

dialog.en: I'm going to eat, shall we meet later?
Sure. What time do you finish?
Around four.
Perfect, see you in a bit.

spanish.use: Say it when you're parting ways and expect to meet again the same day.

spanish.meaning: Give me a shout / hit me up
spanish.note: In casual Mexican Spanish, 'echar un grito' means to get in touch, usually by call or message. People say it when making loose plans or ending a chat.

dialog.es: Voy a estar por tu zona el sábado.
dialog.en: I'll be in your area on Saturday.

dialog.es: ¡Qué bien! Échame un grito cuando llegues.
dialog.en: Great! Hit me up when you get here.
Okay, I'll hit you up.
Perfect, see you there.

spanish.use: Say it when you want a friend to get in touch about plans.

focus.title: Reach out before the birthdays
focus.why: Your calendar is empty today and tomorrow, Paige's birthday is Thursday and Patrick's is Sunday. Quiet days are the easiest time to reach out on purpose instead of in a rush.

idea.line: A short note lands harder than you expect.
idea.body: In experiments, people who wrote gratitude notes underestimated how surprised and happy the recipient would be, and overestimated how awkward the note would feel. The hesitation is usually wrong.
idea.src: Amit Kumar & Nicholas Epley · undervaluing gratitude

dare.title: Plant garlic for next summer
dare.why: Grab one head of garlic, any grocery head works, and break it into cloves. Push them in pointy end up, about 2 inches deep and 6 inches apart, in a pot or a sunny strip of dirt, then water once and walk away. It's sunny and 76 today, and November is exactly the planting window around here; nothing to do all winter, and you pull your own bulbs in June.

place.name: Yamagami's Nursery
place.sub: Cupertino, if you want proper seed garlic

dare.worth: Garlic is the laziest crop there is, and the payoff is a braid of your own in July that tastes nothing like the store. It's also a small bet on being around to harvest it, which is a nice thing to plant on a holiday.

swap.title: Watch sunset from somewhere high
swap.why: Sunset is 4:58 PM. Walk up to the top deck of a parking garage downtown, or the little hill at Shoreline, ten minutes before, and stay until the color is gone. Phone stays in your pocket.
swap.worth: Clear skies today, and the best light of the year is short in November. You'll notice you haven't actually watched one in a while.
